notes.b: Organic compounds fall into families, and what decides how a compound behaves is a small group of atoms attached to its carbon skeleton. The members of one family also change gradually from one to the next.
points: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms, attached to the hydrocarbon part of a molecule (the part made only of carbon and hydrogen), that is responsible for the characteristic chemical properties of a family of organic compounds.
Examples of functional groups are –OH in alcohols and –COOH in carboxylic acids.
The hydrocarbon part, made of C–C and C–H bonds, is fairly unreactive, so reactions take place mainly at the functional group.
Compounds with the same functional group react in the same way; for example, every carboxylic acid fizzes with sodium carbonate.
A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same general formula (one formula, written with n carbons, that fits every member) and the same functional group.
Each member of a homologous series differs from the next by CH₂, a mass of 14, so the chain grows one carbon at a time.

Members of a homologous series have similar chemical properties, because they share a functional group, and a gradual change (trend) in physical properties, such as boiling point rising with chain length.
Each family can be written with R standing for the hydrocarbon part, e.g. R–OH for an alcohol, so that attention falls on the functional group.
notes.tip: If asked what a homologous series is, give the same general formula and the same functional group. For two characteristics you can also use: differ by CH₂, similar chemical properties, gradual trend in physical properties.

notes.b: Each family is listed with its structure, general formula, ending and first member. The first block covers the hydrocarbons, which contain only carbon and hydrogen. There is more on naming alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and benzene in Groups of hydrocarbons and their properties.
points: Alkanes have C–C single bonds only, so they are saturated, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, ending -ane, and first member methane, CH₄.
Cycloalkanes are limited to cyclohexane, a ring of six carbons with single bonds, C₆H₁₂, and it is named with the prefix cyclo- (a word-beginning that tells you the carbons form a ring).
Cyclohexane is a saturated (single bonds only), non-polar (no charged ends) liquid with a boiling point of 81 °C, used as a solvent (a liquid that dissolves other substances).
Cycloalkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, the same as the alkenes, so a cycloalkane and an alkene with the same number of carbons have the same molecular formula.
Alkenes have a C=C double bond, general formula CₙH₂ₙ, ending -ene, and first member ethene, C₂H₄.
Alkynes have a C≡C triple bond, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, ending -yne, and first member ethyne, C₂H₂.
Aromatics are limited to benzene, C₆H₆, a planar (flat) ring of six carbons with delocalised electrons (electrons shared around the whole ring instead of sitting in one bond).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name the family (homologous series) a compound belongs to and to give another member of it. Don't name aromatic compounds other than benzene.

notes.h: Classification table: haloalkanes, alcohols, aldehydes and ketones
notes.b: These families are defined by a functional group that replaces a hydrogen or adds oxygen to the carbon chain. For each, learn the group, the general formula, the ending and the first member.
points: Haloalkanes have a halogen atom, –X (F, Cl, Br, I, the group 17 elements), in place of H, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X for one halogen, prefixes fluoro-, chloro-, bromo- and iodo-, and first member chloromethane, CH₃Cl.
Alcohols have a hydroxyl group, –OH, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH, ending -ol, and first member methanol, CH₃OH.
Aldehydes have a carbonyl group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen) at the end of the chain, –CHO, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁CHO (n = 0, 1, 2 …), i.e. CₙH₂ₙO, ending -al, and first member methanal, HCHO.
Ketones have a carbonyl group, C=O, inside the chain, bonded to two carbons, general formula CₙH₂ₙO (n ≥ 3), ending -one, and first member propanone, CH₃COCH₃.
Aldehydes and ketones share the formula CₙH₂ₙO, so the position of the C=O (end or inside the chain) is what tells the two families apart.
notes.tip: Don't use old trivial names when an IUPAC name is asked: write propanone, not acetone. Ethers, amines and amides are not on the list, so don't name them.

notes.h: Classification table: carboxylic acids, esters and the carbonyl group
notes.b: The last two families both contain oxygen in a –COO– arrangement. Together with aldehydes and ketones, they all share one feature, the carbonyl group.
points: Carboxylic acids (monocarboxylic, meaning one –COOH) have a carboxyl group, –COOH, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH, i.e. CₙH₂ₙO₂, ending -oic acid, and first member methanoic acid, HCOOH.
Esters have an ester group, –COO–, linking two hydrocarbon parts, general formula RCOOR′, CₙH₂ₙO₂ (n ≥ 2), named as alkyl …-oate, and first member methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃.
Carboxylic acids and esters share the formula CₙH₂ₙO₂, so the same molecular formula can belong to an acid or to an ester.
Aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters all contain the carbonyl group, C=O.
notes.tip: To tell the families apart, look at the functional group in the structure, not just the formula. Exams ask you to name the family of a compound.

notes.b: IUPAC naming is a set of systematic rules that gives each compound one name, built from a stem for the carbon chain, an ending for the functional group and prefixes for anything attached. Work through the steps in order.
points: Step 1: find the longest continuous carbon chain that contains the functional group; its number of carbons gives the stem: 1 meth-, 2 eth-, 3 prop-, 4 but-, 5 pent-, 6 hex-.
Step 2: add the ending (suffix) for the functional group (-ol, -al, -one, -oic acid or -oate), or the prefix for a halogen (chloro- and so on).
Step 3: number the chain from the end that gives the functional group the lowest number, and put that number before the ending (butan-2-ol) or before the prefix (2-chlorobutane).
Step 4: name and number branches (side chains of carbon, such as methyl- and ethyl-) and halogen substituents as prefixes, in alphabetical order.
Use di-, tri- and tetra- for two, three or four of the same group, giving each a number, e.g. 1,2-dichloroethane and 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol.
Numbers are separated from each other by commas and from words by hyphens.
No number is needed when there is only one possible position: the –CHO and –COOH carbons are always carbon 1, e.g. ethanal and propanoic acid.
There is only one propanone and only one butanone, so no number is needed for them.
notes.tip: The –COOH and –CHO carbon is carbon 1 and counts in the chain: CH₃CH₂COOH is propanoic acid, not ethanoic acid. Exams ask you to name formulae and to draw structures from names.

notes.b: A haloalkane is an alkane carrying one or more halogen atoms. They are named with the halogen as a prefix, and several are useful solvents and starting materials.
points: A haloalkane is an alkane in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by halogen atoms; a chloroalkane is a haloalkane that contains chlorine.
Chloromethane CH₃Cl, dichloromethane CH₂Cl₂, trichloromethane CHCl₃ and tetrachloromethane CCl₄ are examples, with one, two, three and four chlorine atoms on one carbon.
Further examples, such as chloroethane CH₃CH₂Cl, 1-chloropropane CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl and 2-chloropropane CH₃CHClCH₃ are examples.
Other examples, such as 1-bromobutane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (CH₃)₃CBr and 1,2-dichloroethane CH₂ClCH₂Cl are examples.
Naming example: CH₃CH₂CHClCH₃ has a four-carbon chain with Cl on carbon 2, numbered from the nearer end, so it is 2-chlorobutane.
Dichloromethane is a solvent for oils and grease, e.g. in paint strippers.
Trichloromethane (chloroform) was first used as an anaesthetic (a drug that stops a patient feeling pain during surgery) in 1847 by James Young Simpson in Edinburgh, but it is toxic (poisonous).
Chloroethene is the monomer of PVC, meaning the small molecule that joins in long chains to make the plastic.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to give IUPAC names for chloroalkanes and to give a use of a named compound, so learn one use for each.

notes.b: Alcohols are compounds with an –OH group on a carbon chain. Their names end in -ol, and the number tells you which carbon carries the –OH.
points: Members, such as methanol CH₃OH, ethanol CH₃CH₂OH, propan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, propan-2-ol CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ and butan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH are members.
Other members, such as butan-2-ol CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃, 2-methylpropan-1-ol (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (CH₃)₃COH are also members.
Pentan-1-ol and hexan-1-ol are members too, such as with five and six carbons.
Naming: replace the final -e of the alkane by -ol and give the position of the –OH; CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ is butan-2-ol.
With more than one –OH, keep the -e and add -diol or -triol, so that the name stays easy to say.
Propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol), CH₂(OH)CH(OH)CH₂OH, has three –OH groups and forms the backbone of fats and oils.
notes.tip: Name from the formula by finding the longest chain, putting the –OH on the lowest number and changing -e to -ol.

notes.b: Alcohols are sorted into three classes according to how many other carbon atoms are bonded to the carbon that carries the –OH.
points: Primary alcohol: the carbon bearing the –OH is attached to at most one other carbon atom (–CH₂OH), e.g. ethanol, propan-1-ol, butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol.
Methanol, with no other carbon attached, is also treated as primary.
Secondary alcohol: the carbon bearing the –OH is attached to two other carbon atoms (>CHOH, a carbon with one H and two carbon neighbours), e.g. propan-2-ol and butan-2-ol.
Tertiary alcohol: the carbon bearing the –OH is attached to three other carbon atoms, e.g. 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
The class depends on the number of carbons bonded to the carbon with the –OH, not on the number of –OH groups.
notes.tip: To classify an alcohol and justify it, count the carbons bonded to the carbon with the –OH. Don't use the number of –OH groups or the position number.

notes.b: Alcohols turn up in drinks, fuels and household products, and one of them is dangerous.
points: Ethanol is the alcohol in alcoholic drinks, and is about 40% v/v (40 cm³ of ethanol in every 100 cm³ of drink) in spirits such as whiskey.
Ethanol is a fuel and a solvent, such as in perfumes, deodorants, hairsprays and varnishes.
Methanol is toxic, so it must not be confused with ethanol.
Propan-2-ol is used in hand sanitisers and as a cleaning solvent, for example.
notes.tip: Exams ask for a use or occurrence of a named compound: give the specific use, such as ethanol in spirits or propan-2-ol in hand sanitisers.

notes.h: Aldehydes and ketones: members and naming
notes.b: Both families contain the carbonyl group, C=O. In an aldehyde it is at the end of the chain; in a ketone it is inside the chain, and that difference decides the name.
points: Aldehydes, for example methanal HCHO, ethanal CH₃CHO, propanal CH₃CH₂CHO, butanal CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO and 2-methylpropanal (CH₃)₂CHCHO.
The –CHO group is always at the end of the chain, and its carbon is carbon 1.
Ketones, for example propanone CH₃COCH₃, butanone CH₃COCH₂CH₃, pentan-2-one CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃, pentan-3-one CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ and 3-methylbutan-2-one CH₃COCH(CH₃)₂.
The C=O of a ketone is inside the chain, so the smallest ketone has three carbons.
Naming: replace the -e of the alkane by -al for an aldehyde or by -one for a ketone.
The ketone position is numbered from the nearer end when there is a choice, e.g. pentan-2-one, not pentan-4-one.
notes.tip: The –CHO carbon is carbon 1 and counts in the chain. Write propanone, not acetone, when an IUPAC name is asked.

notes.h: Aldehydes and ketones: occurrence and uses
notes.b: Each of these carbonyl compounds has a particular role, from preserving specimens to flavouring.
points: Methanal in water, called formalin (an aqueous solution of methanal), preserves biological specimens.
Ethanal is the first product formed when the body breaks down ethanol (the first metabolite, meaning the first substance made in the body's chemical breakdown).
Propanone is a solvent, for example in nail varnish remover.
Benzaldehyde gives the flavour of almonds.
notes.tip: Benzaldehyde may be mentioned as a substance, but it is not a naming exercise.

notes.b: Carboxylic acids carry the –COOH group, which is the key to both their names and their behaviour.
points: Members, for example methanoic acid HCOOH, ethanoic acid CH₃COOH, propanoic acid CH₃CH₂COOH, butanoic acid CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH and 2-methylpropanoic acid (CH₃)₂CHCOOH.
Pentanoic acid and hexanoic acid are also members.
Naming: replace the -e of the alkane by -oic acid.
The carbon of the –COOH group is counted in the chain as carbon 1, and substituents (atoms or groups added to the chain) are numbered from it.
CH₃CHClCOOH is 2-chloropropanoic acid, and CH₂ClCOOH is chloroethanoic acid, with no number because the Cl can only be on carbon 2.
The carboxyl group contains a C=O and an –OH on the same carbon, but it behaves differently from both an alcohol and a ketone.
Carboxylic acids are acidic, which is how they differ from alcohols and ketones. There is more on this in Physical properties and acidity.
notes.tip: CH₃CH₂COOH is propanoic acid, not ethanoic acid, because the –COOH carbon counts as carbon 1. Write ethanoic acid, not acetic acid, when an IUPAC name is asked.

notes.b: Carboxylic acids occur in nature and in food.
points: Methanoic acid is in the stings of ants and nettles; its old name, formic acid, comes from the Latin for ant, formica.
Ethanoic acid gives vinegar its sharp taste; vinegar is about 5% ethanoic acid, usually between 4% and 6%.
Ethanoic acid is used as a food flavouring and preservative (a substance that stops food spoiling).
Benzoic acid and sodium benzoate are food preservatives.
notes.tip: Exams ask for a use or occurrence of a named compound. Benzoic acid may be mentioned as a substance, but it is not a naming exercise.

notes.b: An ester is made from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, and its name records both parents, alcohol part first. There is more on the reaction in Tests, reaction schemes and preparing an ester.
points: Esters are formed when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, with loss of water: carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water (⇌ means the reaction is reversible).
Step 1: split the ester at the single-bonded oxygen into the part from the acid, which contains C=O, and the part from the alcohol.
Step 2: name the alcohol part as an alkyl group (a hydrocarbon part named methyl, ethyl, propyl and so on) and write it first.
Step 3: name the acid part by changing -oic acid to -oate; CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, from ethanoic acid and ethanol, is ethyl ethanoate.
The condensed formula is written acid part first, as in CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, but the name gives the alcohol part first, as in ethyl ethanoate.
HCOOC₂H₅ and C₂H₅OOCH are the same compound, ethyl methanoate.
Only esters made from monocarboxylic acids (one –COOH) and primary alcohols (–OH on a carbon with at most one other carbon) are required.
notes.tip: In ester names the alcohol part comes first. CH₃COOCH₃ is methyl ethanoate and HCOOC₂H₅ is ethyl methanoate; they are isomers, not the same compound. Exams ask you to name the acid and alcohol an ester is made from.

notes.b: Esters of the first few acids and alcohols are the ones to know, and their pleasant smells explain most of their uses.
points: Esters of methanoic acid, for example, are methyl methanoate HCOOCH₃, ethyl methanoate HCOOCH₂CH₃ and propyl methanoate HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃.
Esters of ethanoic acid, for example, are methyl ethanoate CH₃COOCH₃, ethyl ethanoate CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and propyl ethanoate CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃.
Esters of propanoic acid, for example, are methyl propanoate CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ and ethyl propanoate CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃.
Esters have sweet, fruity smells and give many fruits and flowers their scent.
Because of their smells, esters are used as food flavourings and in perfumes.
Ethyl ethanoate is used as a solvent in glues and in nail varnish remover.
Fats and oils are esters of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol). There is more on this in Redox and acid–base reactions of organic compounds.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name esters and to give a use or occurrence of a named compound, so learn one use for ethyl ethanoate.

notes.b: Ethanoic acid, C₂H₄O₂, is used to show the four ways of representing an organic molecule. Each shows a different amount of information about the same molecule.
points: Molecular formula: the number of atoms of each element in one molecule, e.g. C₂H₄O₂ for ethanoic acid.
The molecular formula does not show how the atoms are joined.
Condensed structural formula: the atoms bonded to each carbon are written in order along the chain, without drawing bonds, e.g. CH₃COOH.
Branches go in brackets in a condensed formula, e.g. (CH₃)₂CHOH for propan-2-ol.
Expanded (full or displayed) structural formula: every atom and every bond is drawn, e.g. ethanoic acid drawn as H₃C with three C–H bonds, joined to a carbon with a C=O double bond and a C–O–H.
Physical model: a 3D ball-and-stick model, made from a model kit, shows the real spatial arrangement and bond angles.
Model-kit colours are usually carbon black, hydrogen white, oxygen red and chlorine green.
notes.tip: When asked for all the bonds in an expanded formula, show the O–H bond in alcohols and acids, not just OH on the carbon. Skeletal formulae are not on the specification, so use condensed and expanded formulae. Exams ask you to draw expanded structures and write condensed formulae.

notes.h: Empirical formula and ethanol shown four ways
notes.b: The empirical formula is a fifth way of writing a compound, and ethanol gives a worked example of all the representations side by side.
points: Empirical formula (the simplest ratio of atoms) may also be asked. There is more on this in Formulae and balancing equations.
Ethanoic acid, C₂H₄O₂, has empirical formula CH₂O, the same as methanal and glucose.
Diagram: ethanol shown four ways, as C₂H₆O, as CH₃CH₂OH, as the expanded structure with all bonds, and as a ball-and-stick sketch.

notes.b: The shape around a carbon atom depends on how many groups are bonded to it. Carbon appears in three geometries in this course: tetrahedral, planar and linear.
points: A carbon with four single bonds has its four bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron (a pyramid with four triangular faces), with bond angles of 109.5°; this is tetrahedral geometry.
Every carbon in ethanol and in haloalkanes is tetrahedral.
A carbon with one double bond (C=C or C=O) and two single bonds has its three bonding groups in a flat triangle, with bond angles of 120°; this is planar (trigonal planar) geometry.
The C=O carbon in aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters is planar.
Both carbons of ethene are planar, and all six carbons of benzene are planar.
A carbon with a triple bond, as in ethyne, is linear, with a bond angle of 180°; it is neither tetrahedral nor planar in this classification.
An expanded formula drawn on paper shows the tetrahedral angles as 90°; only a 3D model or a wedge drawing shows the true shape.

The shapes follow from electron-pair repulsion: four bonding groups around carbon spread out tetrahedrally, and three groups spread out in a plane, where a double bond counts as one group. There is more on this in Bonding, formulae and shapes.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to identify carbons with planar or tetrahedral geometry and to state the bond angle: 120° for planar, 109.5° for tetrahedral. Cyclohexane carbons are tetrahedral, not planar like benzene.

notes.b: Classify each carbon atom in the molecule. The oxygen that bridges two parts of an ester is not a carbon, so it is not counted.
points: Ethanol CH₃CH₂OH has 2 tetrahedral carbons and 0 planar carbons, because each carbon has four single bonds.
Ethanal CH₃CHO and ethanoic acid CH₃COOH each have 1 tetrahedral carbon (the CH₃, with four single bonds) and 1 planar carbon (the C=O carbon).
Propanone CH₃COCH₃ has 2 tetrahedral carbons (both CH₃) and 1 planar carbon, because only the middle carbon has the C=O.
Methyl methanoate HCOOCH₃ has 1 planar carbon (the C=O carbon) and 1 tetrahedral carbon (the CH₃).
Ethyl ethanoate CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ has 1 planar carbon (the C=O carbon) and 3 tetrahedral carbons, because the other three carbons have only single bonds.
Methyl propanoate CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ has 1 planar carbon and 3 tetrahedral carbons, because only the C=O carbon is planar.
Ethene CH₂=CH₂ and benzene C₆H₆ have all their carbons planar, because every carbon has a double bond.
Cyclohexane C₆H₁₂ has all six carbons tetrahedral, so its ring is not flat, unlike benzene.
notes.tip: Count the C=O carbon of an ester as planar and every CH₃ or CH₂ as tetrahedral. The bridging oxygen isn't a carbon. Exams ask how many of each type a molecule has.

notes.b: Writing R for the part of a molecule that doesn't matter lets you show a whole family, or a whole type of reaction, in one formula.
points: R stands for an alkyl group, the hydrocarbon part of a molecule, e.g. CH₃– or C₂H₅–, so the formula highlights the functional group.
R and R′ are used when two hydrocarbon parts may differ.
General structures: haloalkane R–X; alcohol R–OH; aldehyde R–CHO; ketone R–CO–R′; carboxylic acid R–COOH; ester R–COO–R′.
In an aldehyde, a carboxylic acid or the acid part of an ester, R may be a hydrogen atom, as in methanal HCHO, methanoic acid HCOOH and methyl methanoate HCOOCH₃.
In a ketone both R groups must be carbon groups, and in an ester R′ must be a carbon group, because a ketone's C=O is bonded to two carbons.
Alcohol classes written with R: primary R–CH₂OH; secondary R₂CHOH; tertiary R₃COH.
R is used to show a reaction common to a whole family, e.g. RCOOH + NaOH → RCOONa + H₂O.
notes.tip: For ethanoic acid, the general formula using R is R–COOH, with condensed formula CH₃COOH and molecular formula C₂H₄O₂.

notes.b: Isomers are different compounds that share a molecular formula. Structural isomers differ in how the atoms are joined, and the first type differs in the carbon skeleton.
points: Structural isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae, meaning the atoms are joined in a different order.
Chain isomers differ in the carbon skeleton (the chain of carbons), i.e. in branching: butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol (C₄H₁₀O).
Chain isomers also include butanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid (C₄H₈O₂).
notes.tip: Isomers must have the same molecular formula, so check by counting atoms. Exams ask you to define structural isomers, to identify them in a list or reaction scheme, and to draw and name an isomer of a given compound.

notes.b: Two further types of structural isomer keep the carbon skeleton but change where the functional group is, or which family the compound belongs to.
points: Position isomers have the same functional group in different positions: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol (C₃H₈O).
Position isomers also include 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane (C₃H₇Cl), and pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one (C₅H₁₀O).
Functional group isomers belong to different families: propanal and propanone (C₃H₆O), and butanal and butanone (C₄H₈O).
Further functional group isomers are ethanoic acid and methyl methanoate (C₂H₄O₂), and propanoic acid, methyl ethanoate and ethyl methanoate (C₃H₆O₂).
Cyclohexane and hex-1-ene (C₆H₁₂) are also functional group isomers, since a ring and a C=C double bond give the same formula.
notes.tip: A typical question asks for an isomer from a different homologous series: for propanal, propanone CH₃COCH₃. For an isomer of propan-1-ol, give propan-2-ol CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.

notes.h: Isomer sets and how isomers compare
notes.b: Some formulae have several isomers on the course, and isomers of different types differ in how much their properties change.
points: The four alcohols of formula C₄H₉OH are two primary alcohols, one secondary alcohol and one tertiary alcohol: butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are primary, butan-2-ol is secondary, and 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary.
Esters of formula C₄H₈O₂ on the course are ethyl ethanoate, methyl propanoate and propyl methanoate; the acids of the same formula are butanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid.
Chain and position isomers have similar chemical properties but slightly different physical properties.

Functional group isomers have very different chemical and physical properties, e.g. ethanoic acid (acidic, boiling point 118 °C) and methyl methanoate (not acidic, boiling point 32 °C). There is more on this in Physical properties and acidity.

notes.b: Each way of writing a molecule shows something the others hide, so the best choice depends on what you need to show.
points: The molecular formula is compact but cannot tell isomers apart: C₂H₆O could be ethanol or another compound.
The condensed formula shows the order of atoms and the functional group, so it distinguishes isomers, but it does not show bond angles or shape.
The expanded formula shows every bond, so double bonds and functional groups are clear, but it does not show the 3D shape.
The 3D model shows shape and bond angles, but it is slower to draw, is not to scale, and does not show electron distribution or polarity.
Different representations of the same molecule must contain the same atoms joined in the same way.
In every representation, each carbon must have four bonds, and a double bond counts as two.
notes.tip: If asked what a 3D model shows that a condensed formula does not, answer bond angles and 3D shape.

keyTerms.definition: An atom or group of atoms, attached to a hydrocarbon part, that gives a family of compounds its characteristic chemical properties.
A family of compounds with the same general formula and functional group, each member differing from the next by CH₂.
The C=O group, found in aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters.
The part of a systematic name that gives the number of carbons in the longest chain, e.g. prop- for three carbons.
An alcohol in which the carbon bearing the –OH is attached to at most one other carbon.
An alcohol in which the carbon bearing the –OH is attached to two other carbons.
An alcohol in which the carbon bearing the –OH is attached to three other carbons.
An alkane in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by halogen atoms.
The –COOH group that gives carboxylic acids their acidic character.
A compound formed from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, with loss of water, containing the –COO– group.
A formula giving the number of atoms of each element in one molecule, without showing how they are joined.
The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
A formula that writes the atoms bonded to each carbon in order along the chain, without drawing the bonds.
A formula that draws every atom and every bond in the molecule.
The arrangement of four bonding groups around a carbon atom at the corners of a tetrahedron, with bond angles of 109.5°.
The arrangement of three bonding groups around a carbon atom in a flat triangle, with bond angles of 120°.
The hydrocarbon part of a molecule, such as CH₃– or C₂H₅–, represented by R.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
Structural isomers that differ in the branching of the carbon skeleton.
Structural isomers with the same functional group in different positions on the carbon chain.
Structural isomers that belong to different homologous series.

questions.prompt: Give the IUPAC name of each compound: (i) CH₃CH₂CHO, (ii) CH₃COCH₂CH₃, (iii) CH₃CH₂COOH, (iv) CH₃CH₂COOCH₃, (v) CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl.
questions.model: (i) CH₃CH₂CHO is propanal: a three-carbon chain with the –CHO carbon as carbon 1 and the -al ending. (ii) CH₃COCH₂CH₃ is butanone: a four-carbon chain with the C=O inside the chain; no number is needed because there is only one butanone. (iii) CH₃CH₂COOH is propanoic acid: a three-carbon chain with the -oic acid ending, and the –COOH carbon as carbon 1. (iv) CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ is methyl propanoate: the alcohol part, methyl, is named first, and the acid part, propanoic acid, becomes propanoate. (v) CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl is 1-chloropropane: a three-carbon chain with the chlorine on carbon 1.

questions.prompt: Define primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, and give the name and condensed formula of one example of each.
questions.model: A primary alcohol has the carbon bearing the –OH attached to at most one other carbon atom, for example ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH. A secondary alcohol has the carbon bearing the –OH attached to two other carbon atoms, for example propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. A tertiary alcohol has the carbon bearing the –OH attached to three other carbon atoms, for example 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a homologous series? Give two characteristics of a homologous series.
questions.model: A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same general formula and the same functional group, in which each member differs from the next by CH₂. Two characteristics are: the members have the same general formula, and the members have similar chemical properties. A third is a gradual trend in physical properties, such as boiling point rising with chain length.

questions.prompt: Draw the expanded structure of ethyl ethanoate. Mark one carbon atom with planar geometry and one with tetrahedral geometry, and state the bond angle around each.
questions.model: The expanded structure of ethyl ethanoate is H₃C–C(=O)–O–CH₂–CH₃, with every bond drawn: the H atoms on the CH₃ and CH₂ carbons, the C=O double bond from the acid carbon to its oxygen, and single bonds from that carbon to the bridging oxygen and on to the CH₂ group. The C=O carbon is planar, with a bond angle of 120° around it. Any CH₃ or CH₂ carbon is tetrahedral, with a bond angle of 109.5° around it.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by structural isomers. Draw and name a structural isomer of propanal that belongs to a different homologous series, and one structural isomer of propan-1-ol.
questions.model: Structural isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae, because their atoms are joined in a different order. Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, is C₃H₆O. Propanone, CH₃COCH₃, has the same formula but belongs to the ketone series, so it is a functional group isomer of propanal. Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, has the –OH on carbon 1. Propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, has the –OH on carbon 2, so it is a position isomer of propan-1-ol.

questions.prompt: Write the molecular formula, condensed structural formula and general formula using R for ethanoic acid, and state one thing a 3D model shows that a condensed formula does not.
questions.model: Molecular formula: C₂H₄O₂. Condensed structural formula: CH₃COOH. General formula using R for a carboxylic acid: R–COOH. A 3D model shows the bond angles and the real three-dimensional shape of the molecule, which a condensed formula does not show.
